t: How To Help Difficult Students Who Act Out Due To Emotional Turmoil ue-to-emotional-turmoil/
q: Many difficult students behave the way they do because they’ve experienced—and often continue to experience—emotional turmoil associated with a deplorable home life.
To reach them, your classroom must be a shelter in the midst of the storm.
It has a calming effect that makes them feel safe and valued. Done right, their shoulders will drop when they enter your classroom, their very seat becoming a refuge.
Finger-wagging lectures, dressing downs, sarcastic remarks, and other signs of taking misbehavior personally only work against you and add to their emotional pain.
Rather, with the right classroom management approach, they can begin to heal. They can begin to see themselves and their future in a different light.

t: Going a Bit Deeper with the They Say, I Say Two-Paragraph Template
q: My struggling students have grown increasingly confident in responding to arguments in Articles of the Week, as the template makes argumentative moves explicit instead of vague;

And finally, it's become easier for them and for me to see if they even understand the arguments they're arguing with. Within the first sentences of the template, it's pretty obvious if students get the argument they're responding to. This makes it much easier for me to check their understanding and remediate or reteach where necessary.

So while I love giving my students argumentative articles of the week in part because various columnists model for them, again and again, how arguments work, I've also been learning my kids greatly benefit from seeing the work they're being asked to do modeled a bit more explicitly.

In the model response above, I (the writer) was struggling in the second paragraph with the original template's call for a “for example” sentence. It didn't seem to fit, largely because in the preceding sentence, I had just quoted the article to illustrate why I agreed with the authors. So rather than force the “for example” sentence starter, I did what Cathy and Jerry advise their students to do: I used a different template that fit (in this case, I wanted to elaborate on the quoted material).

But it's like the Karate Kid analogy I used two posts ago: by giving my kids lots of “jacket on, jacket off” experiences with this simple template — and, now, the freedom to modify and adapt it without abandoning the basic They Say / I Say structure — I'm seeking to help them build a neural network of argumentative moves that, once unleashed in later courses that offer less scaffolding, will serve them well.

And to get back to that whole “real writers don't use templates like this” argument: I totally do! Reading They Say / I Say has made me a better writer and arguer — I wish I had been assigned this in college!

t: Why Observation Should Be Your First Response To Misbehavior nse-to-misbehavior/
q: Getting involved too quickly is among the most common classroom management mistakes.
But the truth is, you’re far better off allowing misbehavior to play out.
Merely observing from a safe but noticeable distance, on the other hand, has a calming effect on students, remarkably so, and gives you a better understanding of the facts before responding.
When misbehaving students feel your heavy gaze upon them, when they know that you’re recording their every move, they’ll naturally, almost magically, take a moment’s pause.
Lessons learned on their own, you see, are lessons that resonate deep in their heart, where lasting change happens.

t: How To Rid Your Classroom Of Excitability
q: Spend a day visiting classrooms at your neighborhood school and you’ll find many buzzing with tension.
A consistently tense and excitable classroom is caused not by students, but by their teacher.
A consistently calm personality shows a leadership quality lacking in most adults students come in contact with, and they immediately respect it.
Students tend to take on the personality of their teacher. Outsiders can see this just by spending a few minutes in their company—even out of your presence.
For anxiety and stress have no place in a well-run classroom. They are saboteurs of the highest order, spawning excitability, misbehavior, unhappiness, and a teacher wound too tight to be effective.
x: Pre-class nervousness is normal, but it must be consciously released the moment the school day begins.

t: A Simple, Two-Paragraph Template that Helps Kids to Really Argue
q: The problem with joining in on the conversation is that, although my teenage students (like yours) are passionate arguers in whatever topics they like to nerd out about outside of school — sports, fashion, video games, anime, or whatever — they often lack the tools for entering into argumentative conversations in academic, professional, or civic realms.
Get this: I'm requiring that every student use this template until I see they've fully internalized the moves it contains.
True argument involves building off the ideas of others; it's not simply spouting off your opinion and, if you're really snazzy, giving a cursory mention of what someone else said.

Effective arguers naturally predict what a naysayer might say. Ironically, some are concerned that the Common Core's emphasis on argument is going to create a more fragmented society, but I would argue that nothing is better than argument at helping people to see any given issue from a myriad of sides. I'm not aiming for pithiness when I say that real argument drives people together; I see it in my classroom every year.

This template, in its first sentence, allows me to see if they've got the general argument pinned. It also helps them internalize that the general argument is what an effective arguer focuses on — not debatable side points.

These argumentative events help my students experience how the moves in the They Say / I Say two-paragraph template makes for a more cohesive, entertaining, rigorous debate experience, and that whets their appetite for doing the hard work in writing arguments.

t: How To Keep Your Students Focused The Last Hour Of The School Day t-hour-of-the-school-day/
q: So much good, quality instruction is lost in the hour before dismissal.
The truth is, the last hour of the day takes more out of you than the preceding hours put together.
In this case, ask your students to stand silently behind their desks, feet wide and hands behind their backs. Pause a moment and let their breathing regulate naturally.
It’s critically important that you finish the school day—that is, the last several minutes—without chaos, confusion, or misbehavior
Have your end-of-day routine finish with every student standing behind their desk, silent, reflective, backpack looped over shoulders.
They’ve developed the classroom management skills to keep distractions, interruptions, and time-consuming misbehaviors to a scanty, bare minimum.
